structures.title: Building a basic transitive sentence
structures.explanation: The default Russian sentence puts the subject in the nominative, the verb next, and the direct object in the accusative. Because case endings show the roles, word order is flexible for emphasis, but Subject-Verb-Object is the neutral order. Feminine -а nouns take -у in the object slot.

structures.title: Forming a yes/no or wh- question
structures.explanation: Russian has no auxiliary 'do'. A yes/no question keeps the same words as the statement and just uses rising intonation on the key word. A wh-question begins with the question word (где, что, как) followed by the normal order.

structures.title: Negating an action
structures.explanation: Place the particle не directly before the word being negated, usually the verb. Unlike English there is no helper verb. Russian also allows and requires multiple negatives together (никогда не...).

structures.title: Expressing possession ('to have')
structures.explanation: Russian normally avoids the verb 'to have'. Instead it says 'by/at someone there is X': у + the owner in the genitive + есть + the possessed thing in the nominative. The owner becomes у меня, у тебя, у него, etc.

structures.title: Saying you don't have / there is none
structures.explanation: To negate possession or existence, replace есть with нет and put the missing thing in the GENITIVE. нет always governs the genitive, and in the past/future it becomes не было / не будет.
structures.ex2_ref: There is no metro in the city.

structures.title: Want, can, or must do something
structures.explanation: Modal-like verbs хотеть (want) and мочь (can) plus должен (must) are followed by an infinitive. должен is actually a short adjective, so it agrees in gender/number: должен, должна, должны.
structures.ex1_ref: I want to go to Moscow.

structures.title: Saying where something is located
structures.explanation: For static location use в (inside) or на (on a surface/open area) with the prepositional case, whose typical ending is -е. Certain nouns idiomatically take на (на почте, на работе, на вокзале).
structures.ex2_ref: The book is lying on the table.

structures.title: Real (first) conditional
structures.explanation: For a real, likely condition, use если ('if') with a present or perfective-future verb in the condition clause; the result clause takes the future. No бы is used here — that particle is only for unreal conditions.
structures.ex1_target: Если у меня будет время, я позвоню.
structures.ex1_ref: If I have time, I will call.
structures.ex2_target: Если пойдёт дождь, мы останемся дома.
structures.ex2_ref: If it rains, we'll stay home.

structures.title: Comparing two things
structures.explanation: Form the comparative with the -ее/-ей ending (быстрее, красивее) or with более. 'Than' is expressed by чем + nominative, or more compactly by putting the compared noun directly in the genitive.
structures.ex1_ref: She is taller than I am.
structures.ex2_ref: This building is bigger than that one.

structures.title: Relative clause ('who/which/that')
structures.explanation: который links a description to a noun. It takes the GENDER and NUMBER of the noun it refers to, but its CASE comes from its role inside the relative clause. Always set it off with a comma.
structures.ex1_ref: The man who lives here is a doctor.
structures.ex2_ref: The book that I am reading is interesting.

structures.title: Expressing necessity impersonally
structures.explanation: To say someone needs to do something, put the person in the DATIVE and use надо or нужно + infinitive. There is no grammatical subject in the nominative. Past = было нужно; future = будет нужно.
structures.ex2_ref: He needs to buy a ticket.

structures.title: Giving a reason ('because')
structures.explanation: потому что joins a result and its cause, always with a comma before потому. The cause clause keeps normal word order. To answer 'why?' as a standalone reason, потому что starts the reply.
structures.ex1_target: Я остаюсь дома, потому что я болен.
structures.ex1_ref: I'm staying home because I'm sick.
structures.ex2_target: Она рада, потому что сдала экзамен.
structures.ex2_ref: She is happy because she passed the exam.

structures.title: Forming the superlative ('the most')
structures.explanation: The most common superlative is самый + adjective, and самый agrees with the noun in gender, number and case. Irregular short superlatives exist (лучший = best, худший = worst).

structures.title: Using reflexive verbs
structures.explanation: Reflexive verbs end in -ся (after a consonant) or -сь (after a vowel) and never take a direct accusative object. They cover reflexive, reciprocal, and many everyday meanings (учиться, находиться, начинаться).

structures.title: Expressing purpose ('in order to')
structures.explanation: чтобы introduces a goal. With the SAME subject in both clauses, follow чтобы with an infinitive. With a DIFFERENT subject, follow it with a past-tense verb (this is required after verbs of wishing).
structures.ex1_target: Я учу русский, чтобы работать в Москве.
structures.ex1_ref: I'm learning Russian in order to work in Moscow.

structures.title: Concession ('although / even though')
structures.explanation: хотя concedes a fact that might seem to block the main clause. It usually opens the sentence, and a comma separates the two clauses. The main clause can optionally add но or всё равно for emphasis.
structures.ex1_target: Хотя идёт дождь, я иду гулять.
structures.ex1_ref: Although it's raining, I'm going for a walk.
structures.ex2_target: Хотя он устал, он продолжал работать.
structures.ex2_ref: Even though he was tired, he kept working.
